topic: The Copper Wire Memory of Apollo 11: How Women Hand-Wove Software with Needles
core_thesis: Before silicon microchips could reliably survive space radiation and power blackouts, the Apollo Guidance Computer's flight software was physical copper wire hand-woven through magnetic iron donuts by former textile loom seamstresses at Raytheon.
counter_intuitive_hook: You couldn't download software updates to Apollo 11—every line of code was physically woven with sewing needles into 72 kilobytes of copper rope.
primary_mechanism: A fine copper wire threaded through a magnetic ferrite core induced a current representing a binary '1'; a wire routed outside the core induced zero current, representing a binary '0'. The software program was literally the physical path of the wire.

technical_specifications.rom_capacity: 36,864 words (approx. 72–74 KB) of Core Rope Memory
technical_specifications.physical_durability: 100% immune to cosmic rays, EMP, vibration, and total power loss

facts_and_citations.claim: The AGC's ROM was nicknamed 'LOL Memory' (Little Old Lady memory) because Raytheon hired skilled female textile loom workers in Waltham, Massachusetts to weave the copper ropes.
facts_and_citations.data_point: Months of hand-threading with literal needles per memory module
facts_and_citations.source_name: MIT Instrumentation Laboratory / NASA Historical Data

facts_and_citations.claim: Margaret Hamilton, Director of Software Engineering Division at MIT Instrumentation Lab, pioneered the asynchronous priority executive scheduling that prevented system crashes.
facts_and_citations.data_point: Colossus and Luminary flight software suites
facts_and_citations.source_name: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing

facts_and_citations.claim: During Apollo 11 descent, the AGC flashed 1202 and 1201 radar overflow alarms, but Hamilton's priority architecture dropped non-critical radar cycles while preserving thruster firing.
facts_and_citations.data_point: 1202 CPU Executive Overflow Alarm 3 minutes before landing
